items.text: **Origin:** Arises from the ventral divisions of S2, S3, and S4 sacral ventral rami.

**Formation Location:** Just above the superior border of the sacrotuberous ligament and upper fibres of ischiococcygeus. Leaves the pelvis via the greater sciatic foramen between piriformis and ischiococcygeus.
**Pathway:** Enters the gluteal region. Passes dorsal to the sacrospinous ligament, near its attachment to the ischial spine. Lies medially to the internal pudendal vessels.
**Further Course:** Accompanies the internal pudendal artery through the lesser sciatic foramen into the pudendal canal.
**Branches:** In the posterior part of the canal, gives rise to:
Inferior anal nerve
Perineal nerve
Dorsal nerve of the penis or clitoris (continues anteriorly)

blocks.text: The mechanism of injury (sudden pain on the inside of the knee, feeling a pop, and tenderness along the medial joint line) is characteristic of a medial meniscus tear, which is often associated with twisting movements and trauma.
Structures in the knee and injuries

items.text: **Cruciate Ligaments:** The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is more vulnerable than the posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) due to rotational forces in football. (Options B&D ruled out) Sudden direction changes can overstretch and tear the ACL.

**Collateral Ligaments (Lateral & medial):** Less frequently injured but essential for side-to-side stability. (Option A ruled out) Side tackles (severe adduction or abduction) can strain these structures, leading to tears or sprains.
Medial Meniscus is more prone to injury than the lateral meniscus.
The medial meniscus attaches to the tibial collateral ligament- hence, it is more susceptible to tears from rotational forces.
Bucket-handle tears are common in athletes and are characterised by longitudinal meniscus tears due to pivoting and twisting in a slightly flexed knee.

blocks.text: The patient’s symptoms, including weakness in hip extension, knee flexion, and sensory loss along the posterior thigh and leg, are indicative of sciatic nerve injury. The sciatic nerve originates from the ventral rami of the L4–S3 spinal roots.

items.text: The thickest nerve in the body.
Arises from the ventral rami of L4–S3 spinal nerves. (Option A, C & D ruled out)
Exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis and descends between the greater trochanter and ischial tuberosity along the back of the thigh.
Divides into the tibial and common peroneal nerves above the popliteal fossa.
**Motor:**
**Undivided Trunk:** Supplies all muscles of the back of the thigh (hip extension, knee flexion).
**Tibial Nerve:** Innervates leg muscles (flexion) and foot muscles (plantar flexion).
**Common Peroneal Nerve:** Supplies leg muscles (dorsiflexion).
**Sensory:**
**Tibial Nerve:** Supplies skin on the back of the calf, heel, lateral border of the foot, and sole.
**Common Peroneal Nerve:** Supplies skin on the anterolateral and lateral surfaces of the leg and dorsum of the foot (except for the deep peroneal nerve area).
**Causes:** Penetrating wounds, posterior hip dislocation, pelvic fractures, total hip replacement, misplaced injections in the gluteal region.
**Clinical Features:**
Inability to extend the thigh and flex the knee (hamstring paralysis).
Loss of all movements below the knee (foot drop) leading to flail foot and high-stepping gait.
Loss of sensation on the back of the thigh, entire leg, and foot (except for the saphenous nerve area).

**Sciatica:** Shooting pain along the sciatic nerve distribution (buttock, posterior thigh, lateral leg, dorsum of the foot). Compression/irritation of L4–S3 spinal nerve roots due to herniated lumbar discs.
**Neuropathy:** Entrapment in the piriformis muscle can lead to piriformis syndrome.
